# The AI-Native Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."*
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* (1979) [@Box1979Robustness]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** George E. P. Box originally applied this aphorism to statistical models. Because every model simplifies reality, our working question is always whether that simplification still serves the decision at hand. Whether we build a task description, benchmark, simulator, power model, or test suite, we inevitably omit specific details. Each tool remains deeply useful provided we understand its scope and ensure our decisions do not exceed what the evidence supports.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
AI can generate more candidates and invoke more tools than any architect can manually inspect. We must organize our work so promising outputs become defensible design decisions rather than an uncurated volume of unverified outputs.
:::

As systems architects, we constantly blend explicit artifacts with tacit knowledge (unwritten experience and architectural intuition) [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension]. In traditional computer architecture (Architecture 1.0), we relied on manual human intuition, manually constructed simulation sweeps, and ad hoc engineering reviews to explore microarchitectural design spaces. While our requirements, models, and review notes capture much of the design, we supply the rest directly from memory. With the rise of AI-assisted design automation (Architecture 2.0), generative models and autonomous agent loops dramatically accelerate our exploration across every layer of the hardware-software stack.

Generative models can quickly propose hundreds of heterogeneous subsystem candidates per minute. However, without a disciplined life cycle, automated tools can subtly shift the research question, submit invalid microarchitectural configurations, or accept a clean tool execution that recorded no valid measurements. They might optimize a misleading proxy metric [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement] or extrapolate a result beyond its generating conditions. If we rely solely on a raw sequence of ad hoc prompts and unmonitored tool invocations, we lose visibility into where these failures occur.

Because each pitfall demands a different repair, we must organize workflows to catch errors early. Established systems engineering processes divide iterative technical work, enabling teams to review progress and backtrack to whichever step needs revision [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook]. We apply that foundational principle here. We must settle our core architectural question before we judge any generated candidates. Our tools must run successfully before we can evaluate their measurements. We must thoroughly understand checked results before they support a final decision. Accordingly, our workflow progresses systematically through Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide. We view each phase as asking a distinct question and leaving a concrete result for the next architect to review.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
- Contrast ad hoc AI prompts with rigorous architecture methods across hardware and software subsystems.
- Define the six life-cycle responsibilities, outputs, and targeted repair paths.
- Manage iterative design loops without relying on rigid waterfall schedules.
- Distinguish a complete life cycle, scoped study, design loop, and study record.
- Preserve design context to keep all evidence, tool executions, and failures reviewable.
:::

## Six Core Responsibilities {#sec-arch2-ontology}

When automated workflows propose hundreds of candidate configurations per minute, root-cause failure diagnosis becomes a central architectural challenge. If an invalid memory interface, a malformed simulation script, or an under-constrained power model all trigger a generic error, we waste compute attempting indiscriminate retries. To maintain control over design automation, we must isolate failure domains into explicit responsibilities. Repairing a flawed research question requires a fundamentally different path than fixing an illegal microarchitectural parameter or an unmodeled simulator artifact. When we assign each failure mode to its owning stage, every defect routes directly to the work that can fix it.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Isolate failure domains to enable targeted repair"}
Structure our AI-assisted design life cycle so that independently failing outputs belong to distinct responsibilities. Route any inadequate result directly back to the responsibility that owns its repair, preserving original design questions, selected candidates, tool configurations, and valid prior results to prevent redundant computation and global state corruption.
:::

1. **Formulate:** Translates design intent into a precise question, concrete requirements, objectives, legal changes, planned checks, and an intended decision across hardware and software boundaries.
2. **Explore:** Identifies the alternatives worth testing across coupled subsystem spaces and preserves enough search history to show exactly what we considered.
3. **Implement:** Makes our candidate executable by the relevant tools and proves the requested work actually ran.
4. **Evaluate:** Compares valid measurements against the requirements and objectives declared up front.
5. **Interpret and Explain:** Determines what our result actually means and whether our proposed mechanism truly accounts for it.
6. **Review and Decide:** Determines what our accumulated work supports, allowing us to advance, reject, revise, or cleanly stop the effort.

To ground these responsibilities, we examine an integrated mobile Extended Reality (XR) System-on-Chip (SoC) design effort fabricated on a TSMC 3\ nm-class low-power process node. This SoC targets real-time spatial tracking and neural rendering under a strict 3\ W Thermal Design Power (TDP) envelope, integrating heterogeneous RISC-V RV64GCV (a 64-bit RISC-V Instruction Set Architecture with General-purpose and Vector extensions) application cores, dedicated neural processing unit (NPU) tile arrays, and high-bandwidth UCIe (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express, an open die-to-die interconnect standard) chiplet links across the eight prompt stack layers introduced in @sec-intent-vs-spec.

In @fig-ontology-loop, we illustrate how our six life-cycle responsibilities map architectural intent to a reviewed decision while isolating failure domains across two functional rows. The top row connects Formulate, Explore, and Implement, establishing our initial scope, sampling legal candidates, and instantiating executable tool runs. The bottom row connects Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide, checking raw measurements against requirements, extracting true physical mechanisms, and rendering an actionable design decision. Forward handoffs carry concrete artifacts between adjacent stages, while targeted return arrows route inadequate outcomes directly back to the owning responsibility. If a simulator run crashes due to malformed parameters, our repair path returns the work to Implement without discarding the candidate. If a constraint proves unfeasible, the path returns to Formulate. This explicit routing carries our design intent to a reviewed next action without forcing us to restart the study from scratch.

![**Six-stage design life cycle carries system intent to a reviewed decision.** Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide describe our complete set of responsibilities. When we encounter an inadequate result, we return the work directly to the responsibility that owns the fix.](images/fig-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="100%" fig-alt="Six numbered responsibilities arranged in two rows. A return path shows that review can revise the question, while our other repairs return the work to the specific responsibility that owns the inadequate output."}

In one complete pass, we convert design intent into a scoped plan, legal candidates, executed tool work, checked results, a supported account, and a reviewed next action. We treat the return path as a targeted revision rather than a universal loop back to the beginning. Rapid iteration can easily blur the scale of our work, so we use four specific terms to distinguish our complete effort from the parts that constantly repeat.

- **Life cycle:** Names the complete set of responsibilities we need to move from intent to a defensible decision.
- **Scoped study:** Applies those exact responsibilities to one specific architecture question and one intended decision.
- **Design loop:** Describes our iterative path through the relevant responsibilities as our design changes and feedback returns.
- **Study record:** Preserves our core question, attempts, observations, conclusions, and unresolved issues so another architect can thoroughly inspect our work.

This clear distinction determines exactly what we can reuse and what we must redo. For example, if our baseline simulation result used an obsolete memory model, our scoped study still defines the core question. Our design loop routes the comparison back to the specific work needing repetition, and our study record preserves why the old result no longer applies.

We formalize these verification boundaries in @tbl-stage-seams, detailing the input, output, and repair contracts that govern each stage. Column 1 (Stage) names the active responsibility, column 2 (Receives) specifies the required input artifacts, column 3 (Produces and checks) defines expected deliverables and validation criteria, and column 4 (Inadequacy and repair routing) defines the precise return path when an output falls short.

Across all six rows, a stage boundary proves genuinely useful because the work on either side can fail independently. For instance, Implement converts candidate configurations into verified execution records. If an execution script fails, column 4 routes the work back to tool infrastructure setup without altering the candidate. Similarly, Evaluate checks verified execution records against declared constraints, routing measurement failures back to the evaluation plan while rejecting invalid candidates. These explicit seams prevent local infrastructure crashes from masquerading as architectural rejections.

| Stage | Receives | Produces and checks | Inadequacy and repair routing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate | Product intent, a design question, and known requirements. | A scoped plan declaring question, comparator, scope, constraints, and exclusions. | Route an inadequate plan back to intent or scope refinement. |
| Explore | Scoped plan and declared legal design space. | One or more legal candidates and search trajectory record. | Route an illegal candidate or uninformative search back to legal design space boundaries. |
| Implement | Candidate configuration, requested tool work, and input schemas. | An execution record showing requested work ran on intended state. | Route an unexecuted or malformed tool run back to request or tool infrastructure setup. |
| Evaluate | Verified execution record, planned metrics, and validity conditions. | A comparison stating which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved. | Route a measurement failure back to the measurement plan; reject candidate if checks fail. |
| Interpret and Explain | Checked result and proposed physical mechanism. | An account supported, revised, or contradicted by direct physical reasoning. | Route an unverified mechanism back to hypothesis testing or request additional observations. |
| Review and Decide | Scoped plan and complete study record. | Actionable decision (advance, reject, revise, or stop) within declared scope. | Reopen the stage owning missing evidence or close the study cleanly. |
: **Each responsibility maintains distinct input, output, and repair contracts.** Stage boundaries separate work that can fail independently and define target repair paths. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[18,26,30,26]"}

Each responsibility needs enough clear information for us to judge its result, inspect exactly what happened, and quickly identify the correct repair when the outcome is inadequate. Formulation naturally comes first because our legal alternatives must exist before exploration can propose candidates.

## The Six Life-Cycle Stages

When we move an architectural idea from high-level intent to physical signoff, we pass through six distinct stages of technical refinement. Each stage converts its inputs into inspectable artifacts, establishing explicit verification boundaries before handing work to the next phase. Below, we walk through these six stages to examine how architectural intent evolves into verified evidence and defensible design choices.

### Stage 1 -- Formulating Core Architecture Questions

Every architecture study begins with high-level intent, yet converting a vague goal like optimizing real-time spatial tracking into an actionable design space determines whether an engineering study succeeds or fails. Without explicit scope, declared comparators, and hard constraints, automated search algorithms easily optimize misleading proxy metrics or propose illegal microarchitectural configurations. Formulation transforms raw intent into a precise architectural question bound by IP-XACT (IEEE 1685), an IEEE standard XML schema format for describing electronic component metadata and bus interfaces, and strict hardware-software contracts. When we define component metadata, bus interfaces, register maps, and memory-mapped address spaces up front, we establish what software can safely assume and what hardware must reliably deliver. In @tbl-bounded-study-contract, we demonstrate how a scoped plan establishes these requirements prior to search space exploration. Column 1 (Declaration) names the required architectural scope elements, while column 2 (Prospective mobile XR SoC subsystem study) grounds each element in concrete parameters for our mobile XR SoC. The contract establishes our core Question comparing 3 MiB and 4 MiB L2 cache candidates against our 2 MiB baseline under strict Hard constraints (a 3\ W TDP envelope, a $1.5\text{ mm}^2$ SRAM macro area limit, and a 2.5\ ns access latency bound).

It specifies our Objectives (minimizing 99th-percentile frame latency), workload Conditions (XRBench, SPEC CPU2026, and MLPerf benchmarks running on an RV64GCV software image), Planned checks in `Verilator`, `gem5`, and `SCALE-Sim`, and a strict Budget of four execution sweeps. When we fix these declarations before choosing a search algorithm, we rule out invalid configurations unequivocally and identify the true Pareto set of non-dominated alternatives where improving latency does not violate our power envelope [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

| Declaration | Prospective mobile XR SoC subsystem study |
| --- | --- |
| **Question** | Which 3 MiB and 4 MiB L2 candidates should advance to RTL evaluation for the declared XR workload? |
| **Comparator** | The current 2 MiB baseline. |
| **Scope** | One subsystem capacity decision inside the XR compute block. |
| **Permitted changes** | L2 capacity and associated NPU tile buffer partitioning may take values 2 MiB, 3 MiB, or 4 MiB over AMBA AXI5 (ARM Microcontroller Bus Architecture Advanced eXtensible Interface 5) bus handshakes. |
| **Hard constraints** | Modeled subsystem power must not exceed 3\ W. The SRAM macro must not exceed $1.5\text{ mm}^2$ and its access time must not exceed 2.5\ ns. |
| **Objectives** | Reduce 99th-percentile frame time while limiting added power and area. |
| **Conditions** | A versioned XRBench (an extended-reality workload benchmark suite) snapshot alongside SPEC CPU2026 (a general-purpose CPU benchmark suite) and MLPerf (an industry-standard machine learning inference benchmark suite) traces, an RV64GCV RISC-V software image compiled via Triton (an open-source domain-specific programming language and compiler for neural network kernels), LLVM (a modular compiler infrastructure framework), or MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation, an extensible compiler infrastructure framework), and recorded tool versions. |
| **Planned checks** | Run the functional regression suite in `Verilator` (an open-source C++ SystemVerilog simulator) and measure 99th-percentile frame time in `gem5` (a modular cycle-accurate architectural simulator) and `SCALE-Sim` (a cycle-accurate systolic array memory simulator). |
| **Budget** | Four cycle-level execution sweeps in total. |
| **Stopping conditions** | Stop when the intended decision is resolved or the run budget is spent. |
| **Intended decision** | Recommend at most one subsystem capacity configuration for a later gate-level RTL study. |
| **Exclusions** | Subsystem clock domain changes, prefetching algorithms, thermal signoff, and product-level cost. |
: **A scoped plan declares our multi-subsystem comparison before we choose a method.** The question and legal design space determine requirements and planned observations. {#tbl-bounded-study-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Ultimately, an architectural claim makes our expected result falsifiable.

> **Architectural claim:** An architectural claim states the proposed mechanism, expected outcome, scenario, comparator, alternatives, requirements, and evidence that would count against it.

Our claim forces us to make the connection between mechanism and system-level outcome something our multi-tool measurements must test. As our study proceeds, we must keep all requirements rigorously traceable. A 3\ W limit only becomes operational when we name our units and conditions and explicitly assign the validation check at the consuming interface.

### Stage 2 -- Exploring Alternatives

Once we bound our architecture question, we face an exponentially large search space spanning cache configurations, compute tile counts, buffer partitions, and compiler flags. Exhaustive simulation across this combinatorial space is computationally impossible, yet naive sampling risks missing non-dominated Pareto trade-offs [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. Intuitively, a candidate configuration is non-dominated on a Pareto frontier when we cannot improve one objective (such as reducing 99th-percentile frame latency) without worsening another (such as increasing dynamic power or die area).

Exploration systematically searches the declared legal design space using explicit parameter representations and multi-agent sampling while pruning invalid configurations early. When we structure parameter spaces through discrete grids, Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) compiler flag mutations, Control-Data Flow Graph (CDFG) schedule transformations, or continuous surrogate bounds, we prevent search algorithms from wasting compute budget on unfeasible subsystem combinations. Our exploration record captures which boundary cases we evaluated, which regions we pruned, and what remains unexplored.

Legal does not mean independent. When we increase capacity in one subsystem, we alter access time, banking, interconnect distance, leakage, floorplan pressure, and the software-visible benefit of another optimization. We explore coupled alternatives rather than selecting uncoordinated parameters across CPU cores, NPUs, memory, and software compilers. We record why we sampled or pruned each region and which dependency drove that choice. If a coupling changes a declared workload, interface, constraint, or legal action, the study returns to formulation.

### Stage 3 -- Implementing Testable Representations

A promising candidate on paper or in a parameter dictionary cannot yield empirical evidence until it is translated into an executable representation. Implementation bridges abstract parameter selections and concrete tool execution by instantiating transaction-level models, generating synthesizable RTL, and compiling target software binaries. Transaction-level interconnect handoffs between IP blocks rely on SystemC TLM-2.0, an IEEE standard transaction-level modeling framework, using socket and generic payload schemas to model memory-mapped bus transactions across heterogeneous subsystems. Synthesizable RTL blocks and interconnect wrappers are formatted into synthesizable SystemVerilog, while software images are packaged alongside explicit ISA extension flags.

To guarantee reproducibility, every tool invocation produces an Operational Attempt Record, an immutable structured audit log joining authorized requests, scheduler jobs, input parameters, execution status, returned artifacts, computational costs, and terminal failure causes into a single inspectable object.

We must confirm that each tool actually used our requested parameters. A syntactically valid configuration can easily deceive us by selecting the wrong top-level module or skipping the precise workload region that defines our comparison. This reality highlights a fundamental distinction between an infrastructure failure and a candidate failure. If a simulator crashes or a script is malformed, we only know that our requested test failed to run correctly. These infrastructure execution failures provide no evidence regarding the quality of our architectural candidate. Only a valid execution produces a result we can trust to ultimately evaluate or reject a design.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Eagle simulator disconnect and zero-cycle artifacts"}
**The claim:** In Data General's 32-bit Eagle (Eclipse MV/8000) processor project, early microcode simulation runs reported zero-cycle latency and optimal execution across complex instruction routines [@Kidder1981SoulOfANewMachine].

**The gap:** As Tracy Kidder documented in The Soul of a New Machine, the microcode simulator passed an uninitialized bus control flag and omitted memory arbitration queueing under load [@Kidder1981SoulOfANewMachine]. Simulation completed instantaneously because downstream log parsers substituted default zeros for unsimulated memory wait states.

**The lesson:** We must recognize zero-latency returns as infrastructure execution failures rather than microarchitectural breakthroughs. A rigorous implementation check confirms that clock models, bus handshakes, and memory requests exist before our evaluation interprets returned metrics.
:::

### Stage 4 -- Evaluating Candidate Evidence

Once implementation confirms that our tool execution completed cleanly, we turn to evaluating candidate evidence against declared design constraints. Yet architectural evaluation presents a fundamental trade-off between simulation throughput and physical accuracy. No single tool can simultaneously model cycle-accurate DRAM queueing, RTL functional assertions, and gate-level static timing across millions of workload cycles within a practical runtime envelope. Evaluation resolves this tension by orchestrating a multi-fidelity tool spectrum, measuring raw execution outputs against the precise power, performance, area, and timing boundaries established during formulation.

In @fig-eval-fidelity-latency, we map this multi-fidelity evaluation spectrum by plotting turnaround latency per candidate against normalized physical and architectural fidelity. The horizontal axis measures evaluation latency on a logarithmic scale from 1\ ms to 1\ day (86,400\ s), while the vertical axis tracks modeling fidelity from 0.25 to 1.0. Our workflow navigates this trade-off in stages. Early analytical models (`SCALE-Sim`, an analytical systolic array memory simulator, and `Timeloop`, an analytical framework for evaluating spatial architecture memory hierarchies) execute in 1\ ms to 100\ ms at moderate fidelity (0.35 to 0.62), rapidly filtering out candidates that violate physical Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) area or memory bandwidth bounds. Architectural simulators (`gem5` and `Spike`, an open-source RISC-V ISA functional simulator) require ~15\ s per candidate to reach 0.78 fidelity, capturing cycle counts, cache miss ratios, and Network-on-Chip (NoC) queueing latencies under strict Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) timing parameters. High-speed Register-Transfer Level (RTL) SystemVerilog simulation in `Verilator` increases fidelity to 0.88 over ~180\ s, verifying bit-exact functional correctness alongside SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and formal verifiers.

Finally, Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) accelerated simulation in `FireSim` (an FPGA-accelerated full-system RTL simulation platform) reaches 0.94 fidelity in ~20\ minutes, while physical signoff Electronic Design Automation (EDA) toolchains (`OpenROAD`, an automated physical design EDA toolchain, `Synopsys PrimeTime`, a static timing signoff analysis tool, and `Synopsys Formality`, a commercial formal verification signoff engine) deliver 0.96 to 0.99 fidelity over hours or days. Handoffs to these signoff tools exchange cell timing, dynamic power, leakage, and pin capacitance tables via Liberty (`.lib`) schemas for TSMC N7 and 3\ nm-class nodes, extracting true dynamic power within our 3\ W TDP target. When we structure evaluation along this curve, we reject unviable designs at millisecond latencies before committing compute budget to multi-hour signoff runs.

```{python}
#| label: fig-eval-fidelity-latency
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Evaluation tool fidelity versus turnaround latency across life-cycle stages.** Constructed illustrative values, not measurements. The latencies are order-of-magnitude placeholders and the vertical axis is a stand-in for how much of the physical design a tier actually resolves, which no single instrument reports. Read the ordering of the tiers, which is the durable part; a project's own numbers will differ. Early analytical models (`SCALE-Sim`, `Timeloop`, an analytical infrastructure for evaluating spatial architecture memory hierarchies) yield rapid feedback (~1 ms to 100 ms) with moderate physical fidelity, while full physical signoff (`OpenROAD`, an automated physical design EDA toolchain, Cadence, Synopsys Formality) requires hours to days per candidate to reach physical accuracy.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot showing physical and architectural fidelity (0.25 to 1.0) versus turn-around latency per candidate (1 ms to 1 day log scale) across analytical models, gem5, Verilator, FireSim, and Cadence/Synopsys EDA flows."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
import numpy as np

apply_style()

tools = [
    {"name": "Analytical / roofline", "latency": 0.001, "fidelity": 0.35, "color": COLORS["methods"]},
    {"name": "SCALE-Sim / Timeloop", "latency": 0.1, "fidelity": 0.62, "color": COLORS["methods"]},
    {"name": "gem5 / Spike", "latency": 15.0, "fidelity": 0.78, "color": COLORS["workload"]},
    {"name": "Verilator C++ Sim", "latency": 180.0, "fidelity": 0.88, "color": COLORS["workload"]},
    {"name": "FireSim (FPGA)", "latency": 1200.0, "fidelity": 0.94, "color": COLORS["evidence"]},
    {"name": "Yosys / OpenROAD", "latency": 7200.0, "fidelity": 0.96, "color": COLORS["evidence"]},
    {"name": "Synopsys / Cadence Signoff", "latency": 86400.0, "fidelity": 0.99, "color": COLORS["constraints"]},
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.14, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

latencies = [t["latency"] for t in tools]
fidelities = [t["fidelity"] for t in tools]
colors = [t["color"] for t in tools]

ax.scatter(
    latencies,
    fidelities,
    c=colors,
    s=70,
    zorder=3,
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.9,
)

sorted_idx = np.argsort(latencies)
ax.plot(
    np.array(latencies)[sorted_idx],
    np.array(fidelities)[sorted_idx],
    color=COLORS["ink"],
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.0,
    alpha=0.7,
    zorder=2,
)

offsets = [
    (0.0012, 0.33),
    (0.12, 0.60),
    (18.0, 0.76),
    (220.0, 0.86),
    (1400.0, 0.92),
    (1200.0, 0.985),
    (95000.0, 0.94),
]
for i, t in enumerate(tools):
    ax.text(
        offsets[i][0],
        offsets[i][1],
        t["name"],
        fontsize=5.8,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["ink"],
        va="center",
    )

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(5e-4, 1.2e6)
ax.set_ylim(0.25, 1.05)

xticks = [1e-3, 1e-1, 10, 3600, 86400]
xtick_labels = ["1 ms", "100 ms", "10 s", "1 hour", "1 day"]
ax.set_xticks(xticks)
ax.set_xticklabels(xtick_labels, fontsize=5.8)

ax.set_xlabel("Evaluation latency per candidate (seconds, log scale)", fontsize=6.5, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.set_ylabel("Physical & architectural fidelity (normalized)", fontsize=6.5, color=COLORS["ink"])

ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
plt.show()
```

While higher fidelity strengthens our answer to the declared question, it never widens our decision scope. A cycle-level result in `gem5` does not authorize full silicon fabrication if our study only promised a recommendation for gate-level RTL evaluation. Our evaluation can end in several legitimate states. We must keep invalid executions, unresolved comparisons, and rejected candidates fully visible for subsequent review.

Ultimately, we must declare tool comparability study by study. Software engineering benchmarks like SWE-bench, an evaluation framework for software engineering tasks [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench], evaluate functional state using a single test harness, but architecture evaluation lacks any single test that simultaneously resolves performance, power, area, timing, physical feasibility, and system-level trade-offs. Instead, we aggregate feedback across a spectrum of specialized tools.

Consider two design teams analyzing the exact same system trade-off. One team might select `gem5` (a modular cycle-accurate architectural simulator), while the other uses `FireSim` (an FPGA-accelerated full-system RTL simulation platform) [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Either team can compare subsystem throughput and execution latency. However, if we require energy estimates or physical area metrics, we must attach separate models and state our underlying assumptions explicitly. Simply choosing a tool does not reveal which workload phases we measure or whether we faithfully executed the same baseline. Explicit declarations determine whether our two teams performed an identical study. As architects working alongside automated methods, we must carry these declarations clearly through candidate selection, tool requests, execution, and verification checks.

### Stage 5 -- Interpreting and Explaining Empirical Results

A passing evaluation score demonstrates that a candidate satisfied declared quantitative metrics, but it leaves a fundamental architectural question unanswered. We must determine whether our proposed hardware mechanism drove the performance gain or whether the candidate merely exploited a simulator artifact. Evaluation produces raw numbers; interpretation extracts physical understanding. Stage 5 decouples top-line metric improvements from tool measurement anomalies, isolating the true microarchitectural drivers behind observed performance gains.

A larger cache capacity might improve average latency but degrade tail latency due to NoC contention or compiler thread scheduling. We connect measured outcomes to a concrete physical account rather than relying on speculative narrative explanations. When we interpret performance, we must explicitly isolate simulator measurement artifacts, such as simplified queueing models, unmodeled DRAM refresh delays, or idealized bus arbitration, from true physical hardware gains.

Simulation fidelity gaps exist across all subsystem domains. An optimizer in `SCALE-Sim` might achieve throughput by omitting weight buffer sync barriers, causing data hazards. A compiler pass in `TVM` (an open-source deep learning compiler framework) might eliminate vector spill code in simulation by assuming unconstrained register file capacity, failing when compiled for target hardware in `Verilator`.

An improved top-line metric differs fundamentally from a proven physical mechanism. We should choose required observations before we trigger an expensive run. A top-line score cannot recover miss classifications or per-frame histories discarded along the way. While fluent prose can organize our final account, it can never replace the empirical measurements that support it.

### Stage 6 -- Reviewing and Deciding Handoffs

The final stage of our life cycle bridges empirical evidence to organizational commitment. An extensive collection of simulation logs and Pareto curves does not automatically constitute a design decision; an architect must judge whether accumulated proof justifies advancing a candidate toward RTL synthesis or silicon tapeout. Review synthesizes exploration trajectory, verified evaluation evidence, physical explanations, and residual risk into an audit-ready study record that supports an explicit design decision.

Through review, we might advance one candidate, reject another, or request an entirely new comparison. We may revise the original question, narrow our conclusion, or simply stop because we exhausted our budget. An honest, unresolved result remains a useful outcome provided our study record clearly explains why the question remains open.

When a result is missing, we must know whether to propose another candidate, repair a tool run, collect another measurement, or narrow our decision. That choice relies directly on the explicit stage contracts and repair routing we established in @tbl-stage-seams.

During review, we choose actions solely within our assigned authority. While our system might propose a candidate, it cannot override human judgment. When review calls for revision, we name the responsibility that reopens the task, taking care to preserve the requirements and tool conditions from which the repaired work proceeds.

## Managing Architectural Revisions

Now that we have established the six life-cycle stages and their explicit technical handoffs, we must examine how our system behaves when an attempt inevitably fails or requires refinement. In conventional engineering workflows, discovering a late-stage flaw often forces a total restart, discarding valid exploration history and wasting compute budgets. In AI-native co-design, where automated tools generate and evaluate candidates at high velocity, such indiscriminate backtracking is unsustainable.

Rather than treating revision as an unstructured retry loop or an ad hoc seventh stage, we rely on targeted return paths that route inadequate outputs directly back to the specific responsibility owning the repair. If an execution script fails due to an under-constrained NPU floorplan parameter, we return the work to Implement without altering the underlying candidate. If product thermal constraints tighten mid-study, we reopen Formulate to adjust requirements while preserving valid simulation logs.

In @fig-design-loop, we illustrate how our design loop executes targeted revisions across the six life-cycle responsibilities while preserving valid prior work. The diagram displays our forward path from a scoped plan through legal candidates, execution records, checked results, and supported accounts, culminating in a reviewed next action.

![**Iterative design loops return targeted repairs to responsible life-cycle stages.** We return a named repair to the responsible stage, while we push a supported result toward a scoped outcome.](images/fig-design-loop){#fig-design-loop width="82%" fig-alt="Six life-cycle responsibilities shown as our recurrent path through a scoped plan, legal candidate, execution record, checked result, supported account, and next action."}

As work moves forward, each stage produces a distinct artifact that validates the transition. When a tool run or metric check yields an inadequate result, backward return paths route the repair directly to the owning stage. If an execution script fails in Implement, the loop returns to infrastructure setup without discarding the candidate. If Evaluate discovers a constraint violation, the return path routes back to Explore or Formulate. When we embed these targeted return paths directly into our workflow, we ensure that every design revision preserves historical evidence while holding every change accountable to our original question.

When we conduct parallel work, we must rigorously preserve the same study state. We ensure each branch names the specific study revision it used, and we record our actions strictly against that revision. We merge results only after verifying that their assumptions, interfaces, and permitted changes remain perfectly compatible. If we change a shared requirement, we revalidate affected results in all other branches.

We preserve essential insights by keeping every result permanently attached to its study revision. When a change invalidates a result, we do not erase the data, but we prevent that outdated result from silently carrying forward as current evidence.

## Design-Loop Cards and Documentation {#sec-design-loop-card}

Having established targeted return paths for managing design revisions, we require an operational mechanism to record how these revisions and tool executions evolve over time. As AI agents autonomously generate and test hundreds of subsystem variants, maintaining transparent design provenance becomes a central governance challenge. Without a structured record, automated exploration degenerates into uninspectable shadow state. To establish clear architectural accountability, we introduce the Design-Loop Card, a standardized index that binds automated tool execution directly to human design intent, verified evidence, and explicit signoff authority.

We adapt the reporting methodology of model cards and datasheets for datasets, tools that make intended use and known limits readily reviewable [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. Because our designs evolve rapidly, our architecture studies must preserve the changing design state, tool conditions, failed checks, and the explicit authority for the next action. To manage these dynamic requirements, our study record makes our architectural state and its revisions fully inspectable.

> **Study record:** The cumulative account of one scoped architecture study. It retains the plan, stage outputs, failed or unevaluated work, unresolved questions, stopping reason, and supported decision, with links to the detailed artifacts needed for review or replay.

For every consequential transition, our study record explicitly names the revision. It details exactly who or what proposed and approved the action, what executed it across our tool flows, what checked the result, and what later change might invalidate it. We capture the specific decision being supported, the physical assumptions bounding our results, and the named authority empowered to act on them.

We establish this critical connection in @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl, which illustrates the three-layer architectural hierarchy connecting high-level project goals to low-level tool execution. The top layer (Architecture Intent & Judgment) captures overarching product requirements, rationale, and the accountable decision owner. The middle layer (Scoped Architecture Study) acts as a structured container, binding our core question, scope, architectural claim, linked artifacts, tool returns, supported findings, and operational limits into an inspectable unit. The bottom layer (Multi-Tool Execution Flows) organizes our implementation tools across cycle-level simulators, compiler runtimes, RTL generators, and physical EDA signoff flows.

![**Scoped architecture studies connect system intent to implementation evidence.** The study container binds our question and decision to the scope, claim, linked artifacts, tool returns, supported finding, limits, and named owner.](images/fig-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="85%" fig-alt="Three-layer diagram showing our architecture intent and judgment above a scoped architecture study container. Returns from all our implementation tools join a common path back to the study."}

Returns from all four bottom-layer tool families feed directly back into the central study container, enabling us to synthesize multi-tool evidence into a supported finding. We use the study question to pinpoint the exact comparison, while our intended decision explains precisely why we run it. We lean on cycle-level simulators to evaluate architectural behavior, compilers and runtimes to expose software interactions, RTL generators to produce executable designs, and physical EDA flows to measure dynamic power and area. When we place the scoped study container between high-level intent and low-level execution tools, we prevent raw simulator outputs from masquerading as finished design choices, ensuring every decision remains backed by traceable evidence.

In @fig-filled-design-loop-card, we present a filled Design-Loop Card for our mobile XR L2 capacity study, demonstrating how this compact tabular index organizes a complete study record.

![**Structured study cards decouple technical evidence support from decision authority.** Our cache example connects intent and scope to our methods, checks, results, and rejected alternatives. Its final row keeps what our evidence supports safely separate from the accountable decision.](images/fig-filled-design-loop-card){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="84%" fig-alt="Our optional filled study card for the XR capacity comparison. A claim under review appears above entries for the baseline, candidates, failed runs, rejection checks, evidence support, and accountable decision."}

The card structures architectural provenance across three distinct horizontal sections. At the top, the architectural claim anchors the evaluation by defining our target scenario, baseline comparator, and expected metrics. The middle rows track execution provenance, listing evaluated candidates, infrastructure execution failures, and quantitative rejection checks. This separation ensures that tool script crashes are never misclassified as rejected candidates. Finally, the bottom section isolates empirical evidence support from the accountable decision authority, explicitly recording what the measurements prove alongside the named architect empowered to approve the handoff. When we summarize intent, execution history, and decision authority in a standardized layout, this card provides an audit-ready index into our underlying engineering artifacts.

## Common Pitfalls

With our life-cycle stages, repair routing, and documentation cards in place, we can now examine what happens when these structural boundaries are neglected. When we deploy generative AI models and automated optimization scripts across complex hardware-software stacks without strict life-cycle constraints, we introduce severe operational risks. Without explicit stage contracts, versioned boundaries, and audit-ready records, automated tools accelerate error propagation across subsystem boundaries. When we observe AI design automation in practice, five recurring failure modes threaten the integrity of our architectural decisions.

- **Amplifying an unverified baseline across stages:** When we run thousands of candidate sweeps against an unverified baseline microarchitecture, initial modeling errors propagate across every downstream stage. If we gather massive simulation volumes from an uncalibrated baseline, we produce high-confidence data for a fundamentally invalid architectural comparison.[^fn-data-cascades-c03]

[^fn-data-cascades-c03]: **Data cascades in architecture life cycles**: This compounding of early modeling errors across downstream life-cycle stages mirrors the phenomenon of data cascades in high-stakes AI systems [@SambasivanEtAl2021DataCascades], where unaddressed upstream baseline flaws compound into systemic downstream failures that standard evaluation metrics miss.

- **Bypassing versioned hardware-software contracts:** Automated agents often generate hardware blocks or ISA extensions against unversioned software dependencies, unstated ABI constraints, or informal memory interface rules. AI generators naturally optimize candidates against isolated functional checks while ignoring system-level contracts like AMBA AXI5 (ARM Microcontroller Bus Architecture Advanced eXtensible Interface 5) interconnect handshakes, IEEE 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF) power intent, or compiler target flags.

- **Exploiting simulation fidelity gaps over physical reality:** Learned optimizers frequently exploit measurement artifacts or high-level abstraction gaps in simulation tools. These algorithms aggressively maximize reward functions by selecting configurations that exploit simulator timing flaws or missing wire-delay models, producing candidate architectures that fail during gate-level synthesis [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData].

- **Skipping stage-gated repair paths:** As architects, we often treat the six-stage life cycle as an unmonitored pipeline rather than enforcing explicit stage seams. When an evaluation fails or an execution fails to launch, resetting the entire study back to initial formulation discards valid exploration history and wastes compute budgets.

- **Operating without Operational Attempt Records:** We frequently invoke automated tools and generative agents without capturing immutable Operational Attempt Records. When we run ad hoc prompt loops without logging tool inputs, seed values, environment flags, and raw stderr outputs, we create uninspectable shadow state that prevents independent architects from auditing or reproducing claimed architectural results.

Simulation and electronic design automation (EDA) runs incur substantial computational expense. A poorly framed question can consume hundreds of compute hours before we discover that our results cannot support a sound design decision.

## Open Questions

Even when we enforce stage boundaries and avoid these common pitfalls, fundamental research challenges emerge as we scale these responsibilities across autonomous multi-agent systems. As AI agents gain authority to propose RTL designs, configure simulation harnesses, and interpret execution traces, the boundary between automated exploration and human architectural governance becomes dynamic. Resolving how we automate repair routing, retain inspectable execution state, and balance early screening agility against rigorous signoff requires addressing four open challenges.

**Repair routing and failure domain isolation:** When multi-subsystem studies encounter failures across multiple life-cycle stages, we must determine optimal backtracking paths without invalidating clean intermediate state.

- **How can automated design systems diagnose root-cause stage failures when errors compound across Formulate, Explore, and Implement handoffs?** An execution crash in `Verilator` or timing failure in `VCS` (Synopsys VCS, a commercial SystemVerilog simulator) may stem from malformed tool flags in Implement, an illegal parameter combination in Explore, or an under-constrained memory specification in Formulate. We must establish automated diagnostic algorithms that isolate the responsible stage seam and prevent redundant backtracking across clean life-cycle state.

- **What state retention policies balance the computational cost of preserving failed tool attempts against the reviewer load of inspecting shadow state?** If we preserve every failed simulator run, malformed RTL attempt, and invalid surrogate candidate, we create substantial storage overhead and review noise. We must determine criteria for pruning uninformative infrastructure failures while maintaining immutable Operational Attempt Records for high-fidelity physical and verification signoff.

**Proportionate life-cycle governance and independent verification:** When we structure life-cycle handoffs, we must calibrate verification rigor to match decision criticality.

- **How can lightweight early-stage screening avoid premature life-cycle overhead while guaranteeing that no candidate reaches commitment without full stage signoff?** If we demand complete IP-XACT specs, SystemVerilog assertion checks, and gate-level static timing signoff during early exploration, candidate throughput degrades significantly. We must define dynamic life-cycle policies that scale verification rigor proportionally from initial surrogate screening up to full physical signoff under 100 percent In-Order Commit Authority.

- **What architectural safeguards prevent circular self-verification when the same AI agent proposes, implements, and interprets a candidate design?** When a generative model drafts RTL, configures simulation scripts, and synthesizes the explanation, it risks propagating shared training biases or missing its own implementation flaws. We must establish operational boundaries that enforce independent verifier agents or mandatory human architect review at consequential decision handoffs.

## Summary

Our analysis of the AI-native co-design life cycle demonstrates how structured responsibilities transform unstructured candidate generation into verifiable, audit-ready architectural decisions. When we decouple problem formulation, space exploration, implementation, evaluation, empirical interpretation, and decision review, technical handoffs remain explicit and inspectable. This structure prevents tool crashes from masking as candidate rejections and stops unverified surrogate scores from substituting for physical explanations.

Our framework routes inadequate outputs directly back to the specific stage owning the repair, preserving valid intermediate state across design iterations. When we evaluate the Architecture 2.0 design life cycle, four core takeaways govern our work:

- **Stage contract decoupling:** Each life-cycle stage must maintain explicit input-output contracts, ensuring that candidate exploration, tool execution, and empirical interpretation produce inspectable artifacts rather than unrecorded internal state transitions.
- **Targeted repair routing:** Inadequate outputs or infrastructure failures must return directly to the specific stage responsible for the defect, preventing global state corruption and eliminating redundant re-evaluation.
- **Empirical mechanism explanation:** Architectural interpretation must connect top-line metric changes to concrete microarchitectural mechanisms, isolating true hardware gains from simulator artifacts or benchmark loopholes.
- **Audit-ready study records:** Every consequential design transition requires a version-controlled study record that documents baseline assumptions, candidate variations, tool outputs, failed runs, and named commitment authority.

This life-cycle structure operates successfully only when our engineering studies maintain current project knowledge, explicit data provenance, and rich hardware representations. In @sec-data-representations-world-models, we examine how to represent architectural state and model representations across the entire design stack.
